Muhammad of Ghor: Ghurid sultan from 1173 to 1206.
This far-right, ultranationalist ideology — once called Hitlerism — pushes pseudo-scientific racial hierarchy and rejects liberal democracy in favor of dictatorship. What is it?
On October 7, 2023, the military wing of Hamas attacked this open-air music festival during Shemini Atzeret near kibbutz Re'im, killing 378 people and taking 44 hostage—what was the festival's name?

Nova music festival massacre: On 7 October 2023, the al-Qassam Brigades, the military wing of the Palestinian nationalist Islamist political organization Hamas, initiated a sudden attack on Israel from the Gaza Strip.
Of Junker landowner stock, this 'Iron Chancellor' practiced Realpolitik and engineered the unification of Germany, becoming its first chancellor in 1871 — who is he?
Otto von Bismarck: Chancellor of Germany from 1871 to 1890.
Twice imprisoned during a 1920s satyagraha protest, this Indian activist quit the Congress party in 1925 and went on to found the movement behind modern Dravidian politics. Who is he?
Periyar: Indian social activist and politician (1879–1973)
A former Kopassus special-forces officer, he became Indonesia's oldest first-term president when he took office in 2024 — which leader?
Prabowo Subianto: President of Indonesia since 2024. In early 2008, Prabowo's inner circle established the Gerindra Party.
For three decades this Malagasy statesman served as prime minister and co-king of Madagascar, succeeding his own older brother in the role — who was he?
Rainilaiarivony: Prime Minister of Madagascar from 1864 to 1895.
Before circling the Moon 45 times as command module pilot on Apollo 12, this naval aviator had already flown in space piloting Gemini 11 — which astronaut?
Richard F. Gordon Jr.: American astronaut and lunar explorer (1929–2017)
Appointed Deputy to the Führer, this Nazi leader stunned everyone by flying solo to Scotland in 1941 to try to negotiate Britain out of the war — who was he?

This Indian Army major with the National Security Guard's elite commando unit was killed in action during the 2008 Mumbai attacks and posthumously received India's highest peacetime gallantry award — who was he?
A close friend of Stalin who rose to lead the Communist Party in Leningrad, his 1934 assassination at the Smolny Institute became Stalin's pretext for the Great Purge — who was he?
Sergei Kirov: Soviet politician and revolutionary (1886–1934)
During the War of the Spanish Succession in 1706, Prince Eugene of Savoy's relief of this besieged Savoyard capital — and the death of hero Pietro Micca — became legend; what's this military event?
Siege of Turin: 1706 battle of the War of the Spanish Succession. The Siege of Turin, June to September 1706, took place during the War of the Spanish Succession.
This Italian entrepreneur-turned-politician founded a university in 2006, has presided over a football club since 2017, and became mayor of an Umbrian city in 2023 — who is he?
Stefano Bandecchi: Italian politician and entrepreneur. Stefano Bandecchi (born 4 April 1961) is an Italian politician and entrepreneur.
A Thai Chinese general, he became the only king of Thonburi after leading the liberation of Siam from Burmese occupation and reuniting a country splintered among warlords — who was he?
Taksin: King of Siam from 1767 to 1782.
One of 24 Apollo astronauts to fly to the Moon, he commanded Apollo 10 and, with his crewmate, became the first to fly a Lunar Module in lunar orbit — which test pilot?
Thomas P. Stafford: American astronaut and lunar explorer (1930–2024)
This boy pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty undid his predecessor's experiment with worshipping a single sun-disk god and restored Egypt's traditional pantheon — who is he?
Tutankhamun: Pharaoh of Egypt from 1333 to 1324 BC.
Named for a queen who reigned from 1837 until 1901, this period saw the Irish Famine and the Crimean War against Russia — what was it called?
Victorian era: Queen Victoria's reign, 1837 to 1901.

Sparked by the 1791 Declaration of Pillnitz, this 1792–1797 conflict saw a loose alliance of European monarchies invade Revolutionary France, including the Duke of Brunswick's capture of Verdun — what was it called?
Muslim conquest of the Iberian Peninsula
War of the First Coalition: 1792–1797 wars between France and European powers.
Born to mixed English-American parentage, this statesman led his nation through its darkest hour as Prime Minister during World War II. Who?
Winston Churchill: British statesman and writer (1874–1965)
This Central European nation emerged after World War I as a union of South Slavic peoples, survived until 1992, and was born from the merger of Serbia with a provisional state. What country was this?
Which one below was born first?
Patrick Geddes (born 1854) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is the eldest?
Eratosthenes (born 276 BC) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below was born first?
John Ray (born 1627) is the earliest of the four. John Ray (29 November 1627 – 17 January 1705) was an English Christian naturalist and one of the earliest English parson-naturalists.
Which one below was established earliest?
Cell theory (founded 1839) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below was established earliest?
C (programming language) (founded 1972) is the earliest of the four. C is a general-purpose programming language created in the 1970s by Dennis Ritchie.
Which one below is best known as a physicist?
Luis Walter Alvarez is a physicist. Alvarez devised a set of experiments to observe K-electron capture in radioactive nuclei, predicted by the beta decay theory but never before observed.
Which of these is a chemist?
Chaim Weizmann is a chemist. As a biochemist, Weizmann is considered to be the 'father' of industrial fermentation.
What is the atomic number of Unbihexium?
Unbihexium, also known as element 126 or eka-plutonium, is a hypothetical chemical element; it has atomic number 126 and placeholder symbol Ubh.
In what year was Jean Piaget born?
Jean Piaget: Jean William Fritz Piaget (9 August 1896 – 16 September 1980) was a Swiss psychologist known for his work on child development.
In what year was Alexander Graham Bell born?
Alexander Graham Bell: Bell considered his invention an intrusion on his real work as a scientist and refused to have a telephone in his study.
In what year was Jordan Peterson born?
Jordan Peterson: Jordan Bernt Peterson (born 12 June 1962) is a Canadian psychologist, author, and media commentator.
In what year did John Forbes Nash Jr. die?
John Forbes Nash Jr.: Nash and fellow game theorists John Harsanyi and Reinhard Selten were awarded the 1994 Nobel Prize in Economics.
In what year did Arthur C. Clarke die?
Arthur C. Clarke: Clarke was a science fiction writer, an avid populariser of space travel, and a futurist of distinguished ability.
In what year was Acupuncture discovered?
Acupuncture is a form of alternative medicine and a component of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) in which thin needles are inserted into the body.
In what year was SARS-CoV-2 discovered?
SARS-CoV-2: The virus previously had the provisional name 2019 novel coronavirus (2019-nCoV), and has also been called human coronavirus 2019 (HCoV-19 or hCoV-19).
Furosemide: Pfizer. Furosemide, sold under the brand name Lasix among others, is a loop diuretic medication used to treat edema due to heart failure, liver scarring, or kidney disease.
LIGO: United States. The Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) is a large-scale physics experiment and observatory designed to detect cosmic gravitational waves.
Who is credited with discovering Cadmium?
Cadmium: Friedrich Stromeyer. Cadmium is a chemical element; it has symbol Cd and atomic number 48.
Who is credited with discovering Pigeonhole principle?

Pigeonhole principle: Johann Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet. In mathematics, the pigeonhole principle states that if n items are put into m containers, with n > m, then at least one container must contain more than one item.
Who is credited with discovering Galactic Center?
Galactic Center: Harlow Shapley. The Galactic Center is the barycenter of the Milky Way and a corresponding point on the rotational axis of the galaxy.
First unearthed in Montana in 1987 by a team led by Jack Horner, this horned dinosaur genus takes its name from a Greek river deity — name the genus?
Achelousaurus is a genus of centrosaurine ceratopsid dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous Period of what is now North America, about 77 to 74.8 million years ago.
A military pilot who became the first astronaut representing Turkey, he reached the International Space Station on 18 January 2024 aboard the Axiom Mission 3 flight — who is he?
Alper Gezeravcı (born 2 December 1979) is a military pilot and the first Turkish astronaut.

Named in 1835 from the Greek for 'flower' and 'dark blue,' these pH-shifting pigments paint blueberries, black rice, and some autumn leaves anything from red to purple to nearly black — what are they?

Anthocyanin (from Ancient Greek (nthos) 'flower' and / (kuneos/kuanos) 'dark blue'), also called anthocyans, are water-soluble vacuolar pigments that, depending on their pH, may appear red, pink, purple, blue, or black.
With atomic number 85 and symbol At, this is the rarest naturally occurring element in Earth's crust, forming only as a decay product of heavier elements — name it?
Astatine is a chemical element; it has symbol At and atomic number 85.
Recorded in an ancient Chinese herbal medicine text from around 200 BC and named for a barberry-related plant genus, this yellow-pigmented alkaloid glows under ultraviolet light. What compound is it?
Berberine is an organic compound classified as benzylisoquinoline alkaloid.
This Russian mathematician-turned-oligarch was worth an estimated $3 billion in 1997 after privatizing state assets like Channel One — yet died impoverished and depressed in 2013. Who was he?
Boris Berezovsky (businessman) (23 January 1946 - 23 March 2013), also known as Platon Elenin, was a Russian business oligarch, government official, engineer and mathematician.
Atomic number 20 and chemically akin to strontium and barium, this metal is the most common ingredient in limestone — found there as its carbonate. What element?
Calcium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ca and atomic number 20.
A first-generation cephalosporin that can be swallowed rather than infused, this antibiotic disrupts the bacterial cell wall to treat ear, skin and urinary infections — what is it?
Cefalexin is an antibiotic that can treat a number of bacterial infections. It kills gram-positive and some gram-negative bacteria by disrupting the growth of the bacterial cell wall.
Charted in 1756 by Lacaille and named for the drafting tool that draws circles, this faint southern constellation is easily confused with the mariner's-compass constellation Pyxis. Which one is it?
Circinus is a small, faint constellation in the southern sky, first defined in 1756 by the French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille.
First created in Germany in 1996 and named for an astronomer on his 537th birthday, this synthetic element (number 112) may even be a gas — which one?
Copernicium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Cn and atomic number 112.

Known for names like thornapple, jimsonweed, and devil's trumpet, this genus of nine extremely poisonous, night-blooming plants in the nightshade family can cause hallucinations and delirium if ingested — what is it?
Datura is a genus of nine species of highly poisonous, vespertine-flowering plants belonging to the nightshade family (Solanaceae).
Its name comes from the Ancient Greek for 'female dragon,' and this genus of roughly 200 tree and shrub species now also includes what was once classified as Sansevieria — which genus is it?
Dracaena (plant) is a genus of about 200-220 species of trees and woody shrubs.
What medical condition, caused by viruses like herpes simplex or rabies, bacteria, or autoimmune disease, refers to inflammation of the brain and can cause confusion, seizures, and memory problems?

Encephalitis is inflammation of the brain. The severity can be variable with symptoms including reduction or alteration in consciousness, aphasia, headache, fever, confusion, a stiff neck, and vomiting.
Despite its name, this highly sociable oceanic dolphin earned its label from a skull resembling the orca's — it can reach 20 feet and even forms mixed pods with bottlenose dolphins. What is it?
False killer whale (Pseudorca crassidens) is a species of oceanic dolphin that is the only extant representative of the genus Pseudorca.
He worked on uranium enrichment during the Manhattan Project, then — after McCarthyism cost him his physics post — founded San Francisco's hands-on Exploratorium museum; who was he?

Frank Oppenheimer (August 14, 1912 - February 3, 1985) was an American particle physicist, cattle rancher, professor of physics at the University of Colorado, and the founder of the Exploratorium in San Francisco.

A 1946 civilian demonstrator version of this British fighter became the world's first civilian-registered jet aircraft, decades after it debuted as the Allies' sole combat jet of World War II — which aircraft?
Gloster Meteor was the first British jet fighter and the Allies' only jet aircraft to engage in combat operations during the Second World War.
Caused by a group of enteroviruses, this common infection opens with a fever and then sprinkles blistering spots on exactly the three body parts named in its label. What is it?
Hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD) is a common infection caused by a group of enteroviruses. It typically begins with a fever and feeling generally unwell.
This small rodent, with a pointed snout and a long, nearly hairless tail, has thrived by living alongside humans to the point that truly wild populations are now rare — what animal is it?
House mouse (Mus musculus) is a small mammal of the rodent family Muridae, characteristically having a pointed snout, large rounded ears, and a long and almost hairless tail.
Equal to one-twelfth of a foot and derived from the Roman word for 'twelfth,' this unit of length is often understood as roughly the width of a human thumb — name the unit?
Inch (symbol: in or) is a unit of length in the British Imperial and the United States customary systems of measurement.

This Swiss psychologist's theory of cognitive development, paired with his epistemological views, is together known as genetic epistemology, and remains foundational in early-childhood education. Who is he?
Jean Piaget (9 August 1896 - 16 September 1980) was a Swiss psychologist known for his work on child development.
Arrested in 1995 for various computer crimes and imprisoned for five years, this convicted hacker later became a computer-security consultant and author — who is he?
Kevin Mitnick (August 6, 1963 - July 16, 2023) was an American computer security consultant, author, and convicted hacker.
Caused by Mycobacterium bacteria, this ancient nerve-damaging disease can dull a person's sense of pain so badly that unnoticed wounds cost them their fingers and toes — what is it?
Leprosy (HD), is a long-term infection by the bacterium Mycobacterium leprae or Mycobacterium lepromatosis.
This German physicist gave aerodynamics its rigorous mathematical footing, identifying the boundary layer and lifting-line theory — and a dimensionless number bears his name. Who was he?
Ludwig Prandtl (German; 4 February 1875 - 15 August 1953) was a German fluid dynamicist, physicist and aerospace scientist.
Known by a nickname, this Swedish programmer created Minecraft, the best-selling video game in history, and founded the studio Mojang in 2009 — who is he?
Markus Persson (born 1 June 1979), known by the pseudonym Notch, is a Swedish video game programmer and designer.
What neurological disorder causes moderate-to-severe, often one-sided headaches, frequently accompanied by nausea, light and sound sensitivity, and sometimes preceded by a sensory 'aura'?
Migraine is a neurological disorder that causes moderate-to-severe headaches. The pain usually affects one side of the head.
With shells that are elongated and wedge-shaped rather than round, these bivalves attach themselves to shorelines using threads nicknamed a "beard" — what are they?
Mussel is the common name used for members of several families of bivalve molluscs, from saltwater and freshwater habitats.
A reddish-brown gas that's a key step in making nitric acid for fertilizer, it also seeps into homes from gas-stove cooking and harms indoor air — which compound, formula NO2?
Nitrogen dioxide is a chemical compound with the formula NO2.
Usually caused by bacteria and sometimes requiring amputation in severe cases, this infectious inflammation of bone can be acute or chronic — which condition?
Osteomyelitis (OM) is the infectious inflammation of bone. It may be acute or chronic and can be classified as hematogenous or non-hematogenous.
Commercially produced from citrus fruits as a white-to-light-brown powder, this plant-cell-wall polysaccharide is the gelling agent that makes jams and jellies set — what is it?
Pectin (Ancient) is a heteropolysaccharide, a structural polymer contained in the cell walls and middle lamellae of terrestrial plants.
These drifting, self-feeding members of the plankton community photosynthesize like land plants, so they crowd the sunlit surface waters of oceans and lakes — what are they?
Phytoplankton are the autotrophic (self-feeding) components of the plankton community and a key part of ocean and freshwater ecosystems.
This American actor and mixed martial artist is best known for playing a heroic ranger across a Power Rangers television franchise. Who is he?
Potassium hydroxide is an inorganic compound with the formula KOH, and is commonly called caustic potash.
One of America's top rocketry and high-speed-flight experts, this engineer helped found engineering cybernetics before being deported to China in 1955. Who was he?

Qian Xuesen (December 11, 1911 - October 31, 2009; also spelled as Tsien Hsue-shen) was a Chinese aerospace engineer and cyberneticist who made significant contributions to the field of aerodynamics and established engineering cybernetics.
As chairman of the now-defunct Purdue Pharma, he oversaw the launch of OxyContin — a tenure dramatized in Hulu's Dopesick and Netflix's Painkiller; who is he?
Richard Sackler (born March 10, 1945) is an American businessman, pharmaceutical entrepreneur and physician who was the chairman and president of Purdue Pharma, a now-defunct pharmaceutical company.

Created by Martin Odersky to address criticisms of Java, this statically typed tool blends object-oriented and functional styles, compiles to JVM bytecode, and can even transpile to JavaScript — which one?
Scala (programming language) is a strongly statically typed high-level general-purpose programming language that supports both object-oriented programming and functional programming.
Element number 14 is a tetravalent non-metal sometimes called a metalloid, prized for the transistors and integrated circuits it makes possible — which one is it?
Silicon is a chemical element; it has symbol Si and atomic number 14.
The largest order of reptiles, this group is set apart by movable quadrate bones that let snakes gape their jaws around oversized prey — what's the order called?
Squamata (Latin squamatus, 'scaly, having scales') is the largest order of reptiles; most members of which are commonly known as lizards, with the group also including snakes.

This genus of about a dozen woody flowering shrubs in the olive family, native from southeastern Europe to East Asia, is closely related to privet and provides food for several moth larvae — what is it commonly called?
Syringa is a genus of 12 currently recognized species of flowering woody plants in the olive family called lilacs.
This condition causes abnormally low platelet levels in the blood, leading to prolonged or excessive bleeding — what blood disorder is it?
Thrombocytopenia is a condition characterized by abnormally low levels of platelets (also known as thrombocytes) in the blood.
An important food fish found in marine and brackish waters from the Baltic to the Mediterranean, this flatfish's Black Sea relatives are now classified as a separate species — which fish?
Turbot is a relatively large species of flatfish in the family Scophthalmidae.
Leading organic chemistry at DuPont's Experimental Station, this troubled chemist not only invented nylon but also helped lay the groundwork for neoprene. Who was he?
Wallace Carothers (April 27, 1896 - April 29, 1937) was an American chemist, inventor, and the leader of organic chemistry at DuPont, who was credited with the invention of nylon.

Nicknamed the 'Sleeping Dragon' during his years in seclusion, this Chinese strategist was sought out three times by a warlord before becoming chancellor of the Shu Han state and, later, regent to its young second emperor — who is he?

Zhuge Liang (181 AD - September or October 234 AD), courtesy name Kongming, was a Chinese statesman and strategist who lived through the collapse of the Eastern Han dynasty and became the principal architect of the Shu Han state.
This nucleoside, a building block of RNA, gives rise to the energy carriers ATP and ADP and is used as an intravenous drug for certain irregular heartbeats — what is it?
Working at a Soviet computing centre in 1985, this engineer designed one of history's most famous puzzle games — yet saw no royalties from it until founding a company around it in 1996. Who is he?
Caused by the parasite Entamoeba histolytica, this intestinal infection can spread to the liver and trigger abscesses there even without any prior diarrhea — what condition is it?
Amoebiasis: Human disease caused by amoeba protists.

Their larvae — nicknamed "doodlebugs" in North America for the marks they leave — dig sandy pits to trap passing ants, while the dusk-flying adults are often mistaken for dragonflies. What insect is this?
His namesake effect — scattered X-rays losing energy — proved light behaves as particles and earned a share of the 1927 Nobel Prize in Physics. Who was this American physicist?
Discovered by Robert Koch in 1876, this rod-shaped microbe was the first ever shown experimentally to cause disease, providing the earliest evidence for germ theory — which organism?
Once chairman of the Nasdaq, this financier admitted to masterminding the largest-known Ponzi scheme in history, estimated at $65 billion — who is it?
Bernie Madoff: American financier and con artist (1938–2021)

Developed to supplement the 727 on short routes, this narrow-body twinjet kept the 707's fuselage width and six-abreast seating and entered service with Lufthansa in 1968 — which best-selling aircraft is it?
A tree-like cluster of dark-green flower heads sprouting from a thick pale stalk, this cabbage-family vegetable is a close cousin of cauliflower and can be eaten raw or cooked — what is it?
Broccoli: Edible green plant in the cabbage family.
Named to honor the Virgin Mary and her golden crown, this daisy-family flower is also known as the pot marigold — which plant?
Calendula officinalis: Species of flowering plant in the daisy family Asteraceae.
Known also as yoke elm, this species of hornbeam native to Western Asia and Europe grows only up to elevations of about 1,000 metres — which species?
Carpinus betulus: Species of tree. It requires a warm climate for good growth, and occurs only at elevations up to 1,000 metres (3,300 ft).
Often called 'the father of the computer,' this English polymath designed the difference engine and the analytical engine, borrowing a punch-card principle from the Jacquard loom — who is he?
Charles Babbage: English mathematician, philosopher, and engineer (1791–1871)
One of the original citrus fruits, this large fragrant relative of the lemon has a thick, coarse rind and is a genetic ancestor of most modern citrus hybrids — what is it?
In mathematics, this is a selection of items from a set where the order of choosing them does not matter, unlike a permutation — what is it called?

Combination: Selection of items from a set. In mathematics, a combination is a selection of items from a set that has distinct members, such that the order of selection does not matter (unlike permutations).
Going by puma, mountain lion, catamount, and panther depending on where you stand, this big cat is the most widely distributed wild land mammal in the Americas — what is it?
Cougar: Wild cat species native to the Americas.
Native to Mexico and Central America, this tuberous flowering plant blooms in nearly every hue except blue, and its tubers store energy as inulin rather than starch — what is it?
Dahlia: Genus of flowering plants in the daisy family Asteraceae.

Historically defined by having two embryonic seed leaves, this once-standard division of flowering plants covers around 200,000 species but turned out not to share one common ancestor — which plant group?
Dicotyledon: Historical grouping of flowering plants.
One of the very first vertebrate apex predators on Earth, this armor-plated, jointed-neck fish patrolled open Devonian seas some 380 million years ago — which genus?
Born in Pretoria and once a Zip2 co-founder, this CEO of Tesla and SpaceX became, by some estimates, the first dollar trillionaire in 2026 — who is he?
Elon Musk: Businessman and public official (born 1971)
Also called moral philosophy, this field splits into normative, applied, and meta- branches as it asks what people ought to do and whether objective moral facts even exist. Which discipline is it?
Proposed in 1724 by a physicist who set water's freezing point at 32 degrees and boiling at 212, this temperature scale was originally anchored to a freezing brine solution — which scale?
Fahrenheit: Temperature scale. The Fahrenheit scale is a temperature scale based on one proposed in 1724 by the physicist Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit (1686–1736).
Lacking a body cavity and equipped with just one opening for both eating and excreting, these simple unsegmented invertebrates are named for their shape — what are they?
Marketed as Neurontin, this anticonvulsant and GABA derivative is prescribed for nerve pain and partial seizures by binding to the α2δ subunits of calcium channels — what is it?
Caught from contaminated water and common among travelers and children, this parasitic infection causes fatty, sticky diarrhea weeks after exposure — what is it?
Giardiasis: Parasitic disease that results in diarrhea.
With a black head, white cheeks and yellow underparts, this widespread European songbird was split from two Asian relatives after 2005 DNA studies?
Great tit: Passerine bird in the tit family Paridae.

Nicknamed the 'Halloween beetle' in North America for invading homes each October to overwinter, this extremely color-variable insect was introduced there from eastern Asia to control aphids — what species is it?
Harmonia axyridis: Species of beetle. Harmonia axyridis is a lady beetle or ladybird species that is most commonly known as the harlequin, Asian, or multicoloured Asian lady beetle.
Known scientifically as singultus, this involuntary diaphragm spasm closes the glottis in about 35 milliseconds to produce a signature sound — what reflex is it?
Hiccup: Involuntary contraction of the diaphragm. The rhythm of the hiccup, or the time between hiccups, tends to be relatively constant.

Made of one oxygen and one hydrogen atom bonded together with a negative charge, this ion is the active base in the sodium compound used to produce millions of tons of industrial chemicals yearly. What ion is it?
Patented in 1961 and used to fight fever, pain and inflammation by blocking the cyclooxygenase enzyme, this drug sits on the WHO's List of Essential Medicines — what is it?
Before he proposed that the Earth behaves like one self-regulating living system, this English independent scientist built the detector that first revealed CFCs lurking in our atmosphere. Who was he?
A former Navy SEAL turned physician, this NASA astronaut flew to the International Space Station in 2025 as part of Expedition 72/73 after earning a Silver Star for valor in combat — who is he?
Jonny Kim: American astronaut, physician, and former U.S. Navy SEAL (born 1984)
This Gram-negative rod bacterium can turn deadly if aspirated into the lungs, producing a telltale bloody, brownish-yellow jelly-like sputum — which pathogen?
Klebsiella pneumoniae: Species of bacterium. Klebsiella pneumoniae is a Gram-negative, non-motile, encapsulated, lactose-fermenting, facultative anaerobic, rod-shaped bacterium.

Named from the Greek word for 'honey bee' because its flowers attract them, this citrus-scented herb in the mint family has been cultivated since at least the 16th century for tea and aromatic oils — what is it?

Three of this crustacean's five pairs of legs bear claws, with the first pair often dramatically oversized, and its burrow-dwelling relatives include the Norway variety known as langoustine - which creature?
Lobster: Family of clawed marine crustaceans.
With deeply forked tails and iridescent, tiger-like stripes on their backs, these pelagic fish migrate in huge schools to shallow coastal spawning grounds — what are they?
Mackerel: Pelagic fish. Mackerel is a common name applied to a number of different species of pelagic fish, mostly from the family Scombridae.

In 1835 this Scottish polymath and Caroline Herschel became the first female Honorary Members of the Royal Astronomical Society, and she signed first on John Stuart Mill's 1866 petition for women's suffrage — who was she?

Diagnosed when a person has at least three of five red flags -- including abdominal obesity and high blood pressure -- this cluster of conditions raises the risk of heart disease and diabetes in about a quarter of US adults. What is it?
Metabolic syndrome: Cluster of diseases occurring with obesity.
Nicknamed the 'sensitive plant,' this legume's leaves fold inward within seconds of being touched and reopen a few minutes later — what plant is it?
Mimosa pudica: Species of creeping annual plant.
Serving King Roger II in Norman Sicily, this Arab geographer created the Tabula Rogeriana, one of the most advanced world maps of the medieval era — who was he?
Known in Sanskrit as Padma or Kamala, this aquatic plant is often called sacred lotus though true water lilies actually belong to a different family — what species?
Nelumbo nucifera: Species of aquatic flowering plant. It is sometimes colloquially called a water lily, though this more often refers to members of the family Nymphaeaceae.
Designed in the late 1950s as a privately funded project, this small twin-engine fighter was built cheap to buy and maintain, making it a hugely popular export jet — what is it?
Northrop F-5: US lightweight low-cost fighter aircraft.
Named by analogy to how organs serve the body, what term describes a specialized, function-specific subunit within a biological cell?

Organelle: Specialized subunit within a cell. The name organelle comes from the idea that these structures are parts of cells, as organs are to the body, hence organelle, the suffix -elle being a diminutive.
Often triggered by nail-biting or frequent hand-washing, this inflammation of the skin around the nail is usually bacterial when sudden and fungal when it drags on — what is it called?
Paronychia: Inflammation of skin surrounding a nail. Its sudden (acute) occurrence is usually due to the bacterium Staphylococcus aureus.
Discovered in 1972 and used to treat scabies and lice, this pyrethroid insecticide is safe for most mammals but especially dangerous to cats, who metabolize it slowly — what is it?
Permethrin: Medication and insecticide. It is applied to the skin as a cream or lotion.
Domesticated twice in the Neolithic — once near the Tigris Basin and once in China — this even-toed, hoofed omnivore is farmed mainly for pork; what is it?

In this group of disorders, pigment-like substances called porphyrins accumulate in the body, triggering attacks of abdominal pain, confusion, and even seizures that can be set off by alcohol or fasting. What is it?
Porphyria: Metabolic disorders in which porphyrins build up in the body.
Nicknamed the 'liberty cap' for its distinctive conical shape, this psychoactive mushroom grows in grassland and produces psilocybin — what is it?
Psilocybe semilanceata: Species of fungus in the family Hymenogastraceae, native to Europe.
This Indian social activist founded the Azadi Bachao Andolan and later teamed with yoga guru Ramdev to promote swadeshi economics — who was he?
Rajiv Dixit: Indian activist. Rajiv Dixit (30 November 1967 – 30 November 2010) was an Indian social activist who founded the Azadi Bachao Andolan.
His 'Essai Sur La Nature Du Commerce' was called the 'cradle of political economy'; this Irish-French banker made a fortune speculating in John Law's Mississippi Company — who is it?
Richard Cantillon: Irish-French economist and banker (c. 1680 – 1734)
This light Swedish single-engine supersonic fighter has a delta wing and canard configuration with fly-by-wire controls and is fully NATO interoperable — what is it?
Saab JAS 39 Gripen: Light single-engined multirole fighter aircraft from Sweden.
Living on ocean floors worldwide, this leathery-skinned echinoderm recycles nutrients as a detritivore and is named for its resemblance to a common garden vegetable — what is it?

Also called carborundum, this hard compound occurs in nature as the rare mineral moissanite but has been mass-produced as an abrasive since 1893 — and it stiffens disc brakes and bulletproof vests; what is it?
Silicon carbide: Wide-bandgap semiconductor and abrasion-resistant ceramic.
Known by nicknames like 'garden' and 'lamb,' and native from Ireland to southern China, which herb's aromatic oil flavors food, teas, and various scents?
Spearmint: Plant species in the mint family.

Metro AG: Otto Beisheim. As of September 2025, Metro is operating 622 wholesale stores in 21 countries.
Oyo Rooms: Ritesh Agarwal. Founded in 2012 by Ritesh Agarwal, OYO initially consisted mainly of budget hotels.
Nike, Inc.: Phil Knight. Nike, Inc. is an American athletic footwear and apparel corporation headquartered near Beaverton, Oregon.
U.S. Steel: Andrew Carnegie. Steel was acquired by Nippon Steel in a deal arranged with the United States government.
In which country is Capgemini based?
Capgemini: France. Capgemini SE is a French multinational information technology (IT) services and consulting company.
In which country is Baidu based?
Baidu: People's Republic of China. Besides its core internet search business, Baidu has also diversified into other areas.
In which country is HSBC based?
HSBC: United Kingdom. According to S&P Global's April 2026 report, HSBC is Europe's 2nd largest bank by assets, with $3.212 trillion in assets.
7-Eleven: United States. 7-Eleven, Inc. is an American convenience store chain headquartered in Irving, Texas.
In which country is Jack Daniel's based?

In which country is Ekşi Sözlük?
Ekşi Sözlük: Turkey. It is one of the largest online communities in Turkey and one of the oldest Turkish websites still in operation.
In which country is Lay's based?
Lay's: United States. The name derives from "Lay", the surname of the founder of the company originally formed in 1938 to produce potato chips.

Formed in 1988 by merging a Swedish electrical firm with a Swiss counterpart, this dual-listed technology company focused on electrification and automation has spent three decades on the Fortune Global 500 — name it?
ABB is a Swedish-Swiss technology company, that operates in the fields of electrification and automation.
Headquartered in Stockholm and founded in 1910, this Swedish company is consistently ranked the world's second-largest home appliance maker by units sold, behind only Whirlpool — what is it?
Electrolux (originally Elektromekaniska AB and later Elektrolux AB) is a Swedish multinational home appliance manufacturer, headquartered in Stockholm.
This Swiss running-shoe brand controlled 40 percent of Switzerland's running-shoe market in 2019 and is approaching a $20 billion valuation by 2025 — which brand?
On (company) is a Swiss athletic shoe and performance sportswear company that designs and markets sports clothing and running shoes.
Headquartered in both Massachusetts and Florida, which workforce-management software company's name stands for Ultimate Kronos Group?
UKG is an American multinational technology company with dual headquarters in Lowell, Massachusetts, and Weston, Florida.
This British oil-and-gas "supermajor" traces its origins to the 1909 Anglo-Persian Oil Company and later went by the name British Petroleum — which company is it?
BP: British multinational oil and gas company. BP p.l.c. is a British multinational oil and gas company headquartered in London, England.
Founded in London in 1845 by an accountant of the same name, this Big Four firm is now the largest professional-services network in the world by revenue and headcount — which one?
Deloitte: Multinational professional services network. The firm was founded by the accountant William Welch Deloitte in London, England in 1845 and expanded into the United States in 1890.
Founded in a one-car Palo Alto garage in 1939 by two Stanford engineers, this tech company grew into a Silicon Valley powerhouse before splitting into two separate companies in 2015 — which company?
Founded in 1998 as a yoga-pants retailer, this Vancouver-headquartered athletic apparel company now runs more than 760 stores worldwide — which brand?
Lululemon: Multinational athletic apparel retailer. The company has 767 stores (as of fiscal year 2024) and also processes sales online through its website.
Marlboro's parent tobacco giant, spun off from Altria in 2008, saw its Iqos brand overtake Marlboro in revenue by late 2023 — which company?
Philip Morris International: Multinational tobacco company. Philip Morris International Inc. (PMI) is a tobacco company, with products sold in over 180 countries.
Founded in 1967 by Herb Kelleher and Rollin King and headquartered at Dallas's Love Field, which major U.S. carrier flies an all-Boeing 737 fleet?
Southwest Airlines: Airline of the United States.
One of America's 'Big Four' banks, this company's main office in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, makes it a legal 'citizen' of that state in most federal courts — which bank is this?
Wells Fargo: American multinational banking and financial services company.
